items.title: Jang interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2013
items.q: The 'Japanese girl' is mentioned by the interviewer as a hypothetical or general example ('a Japanese girl living in China') to frame a question about cultural roots; the interviewee does not claim to have met, known, or collaborated with this specific individual.

ctx.x: And when she was studying piano she was learning Western — Bach. And I just thought what an interesting — a Japanese girl living in China, but she’s studying European music and it wasn’t until she went back to Japan around the end of World War II that she learned jazz. But she had — to make a long story short — she had to specifically seek out her own roots. So I’m wondering how and when did you get to explore — how did you explore traditional Chinese melodies which I assume that you wanted to include?

Well it took a lot of time. Because you see I also took ethnomusicology courses at Oberlin. And I was searching for those Chinese folk songs. But you have to understand that ethnomusicology, which was a marginalized field at that time, like they had a one- person faculty trying to do everything, and still today, you know, I mean for a long time you had everything except China, which is a large country, and maybe it was the political relationship between the U.S. and China, but if we even look specifically at the…
